idiom_name: file-scope instance table + accessor; opaque handle in the header; pthread_mutex for the per-key insert
implementation_notes: C has no classes and no module privacy, so the multiton becomes a translation-unit idiom: a file-scope static table (an array of {key, handle} entries, or a small map) that only the .c file can touch, an opaque handle type declared in the header, and one exported accessor get_conn(key) that links the entry on a miss. The per-key find-or-insert must happen under a single pthread_mutex_t; pthread_once or C11 call_once/once_flag guards the table's one-time initialisation only, not the per-key creation, so they do not remove the mutex. The classic structure is the only option here - C has nothing to replace it with - and it is justified whenever several parts of a C program need the same keyed resource.
pitfalls: pthread_once/call_once make the table's construction exactly-once, not the per-key find-or-insert: the accessor still needs its mutex, or two threads open two connections for one key.
A fixed-size table must fail loudly when it is full - overwriting an entry silently orphans the instance it held, and callers keep a pointer to it.
Keys must be copied or interned into table-owned storage: keeping a caller's pointer (or a stack buffer) leaves dangling keys after the call returns.
The table itself is not thread-safe against iteration: any shutdown path that walks it to close instances must hold the same mutex.
